title: Table D, Graded Return to Run Program for Bone Stress Injury (adapted from Warden et al 2016), BJSM blog
authors: BJSM blog (adapted from Warden et al 2016)
population: Athletes returning to running after bone stress injury; no outcome data
findings: Monitoring: symptom free during the run, after it and the next day; if symptoms are provoked, stop the session and regress to the previous stage following a rest day.
Stage 1 (jog at 50% slower than usual pace, rest day between every session): a 30-min walk, then walk 9 / jog 1, 8/2, 7/3, 6/4, 4/6 and 2/8 (each x3 = 30 min), i.e. 6 run-walk sessions.
Stage 2 (easy running, rest day between): jog 30 min (50%), then run 30 min at 60%, 70%, 80%, 90% and full pace. Stage 3: running on consecutive days 'if appropriate' (2 days on, 1 off).
Stage 4: gradual progression with weekly volume +10-20%, rest days and energy intake increased with expenditure.
limitations: Expert-opinion protocol for bone stress injury (D); no outcome data; the original Warden source was not fetched; the PDF date comes from the file metadata (created May 2019) and URL path.
implications: For a runner returning from a bone stress injury, the clinical protocol starts at 1 min of jogging in 10, every other day, and reaches 30 min continuous after 6 run-walk sessions; for that specific flag a 3 x 20 floor is far too high.
The protocol is specific to bone stress injury; whether it applies to a generic 'recent injury' flag is the plan designer's extrapolation, not a finding.
Post-protocol ramp is +10-20% weekly volume; the ramp rule does not say a floor week is exempt.

verification.notes: Re-downloaded the one-page PDF and read it with pdftotext. Stages 1-4 and monitoring text match; PDF creation date is 7 May 2019. Softened the implications: protocol applies to bone stress injury only, and the 'floor exempt from ramp' point was not supported by the source. Practice source (programme, coaching or clinical page): a published convention, not evidence; grade D.

interests: None found: a clinical table hosted on a journal's blog (BMJ); the hosting post's author is a physiotherapist and states no commercial stake.

r1.note: Every stage and the monitoring text located in the one-page PDF fetched 2026-10-31 (file created 2019-05-07, text layer read with pdftotext); the hosting BJSM blog post of 2019-05-08 was read to find the table's author and context.

r2.note: The table is unsigned. The hosting post is by Anna Boniface, a physiotherapist and marathon runner per the BMJ blog's own bio, and credits Warden et al (Indiana University per Europe PMC). No independent record of Boniface's credential was found, and the original Warden table was not read (the JOSPT page answered with a bot check), so how much of the table is Warden's is unknown.

r3.note: PDF created 2019-05-07. The post links a later upload (Table C, created 2019-05-08) with the same stages 1 to 3, so this file is the earlier of two. The table cites Warden 2016 while the post's reference list gives Warden 2014 (JOSPT). Later corpus papers (warden-2021-bsi-optimal-workload, george-2024-tibial-bsi-return-to-run) give no durations and do not supersede it.

r4.note: Structure (graded walk-run levels, rest day between runs, regress on symptoms) agrees with george-2024-tibial-bsi-return-to-run (graduated programme, symptom-led) and with the Sanford tendon table (sanford-2024). Durations have no second source; the conservative reading takes the lesser of the level and the G-3 limit, as the Param notes state.

r5.note: Population is athletes with bone stress injury; the record and the injuryReturn Param note label use for a generic injury flag as an extrapolation.

r6.note: Evidence level D, at the practice cap.
